questions.q:
Kabir in Bhopal grows a tomato sapling in a pot on a covered balcony where direct sunlight never reaches. His mother waters it daily. A neighbour's sapling, kept on an open terrace and watered the same way, is taller. Kabir's grandfather says, 'Water it twice a day and it will catch up.' His cousin says, 'Then stop watering and put it in the sun; the sun will feed it.'
(a) Which pot of Activity 10.1 is Kabir's sapling like, and what is expected after two weeks?
(b) Evaluate the grandfather's advice.
(c) Evaluate the cousin's advice.
(d) What should Kabir do?
questions.a: (a) It is like pot C and is expected to grow less than a sunlit, watered plant. (b) Partly right: water is needed, but extra water cannot replace sunlight (pot C is watered daily and still grows less). (c) Partly right: sunlight is needed, but without water the plant is like pot B and may die. (d) Move the pot into direct sunlight and keep watering it, because plants need both.
s: Part (a): pot C, grows less
Part (b): water needed but cannot replace sunlight
Part (c): sunlight needed but stopping water is like pot B
Part (d): sunlight plus continued watering

questions.q:
A student compares a sunlit watered sapling X with a sunlit sapling Y that gets no water.
(a) Which factor is she testing?
(b) She now wants to test sunlight using X. Describe the second pot's conditions and say why also stopping its water would spoil the test.
questions.a: (a) Water. (b) A second pot with the same sapling and water, kept in the dark. If its water were also stopped, two conditions would change and the effect of sunlight alone could not be judged.
s: Part (a): water
Part (b): dark pot with water, and only one condition changed

questions.q: Priya says: 'The sapling in pot C will still grow a little, though less than the one in pot A, because it gets water.' Do you agree? Explain with Activity 10.1.
questions.a: Yes. Pot C gets water but no sunlight, and the book says its plant grows less than pot A, not that it fails to grow. This also shows sunlight is needed for better growth.
s: Verdict: agrees
Pot C has water but no sunlight and grows less than pot A
Conclusion: sunlight is needed for good growth

questions.q:
A school in Ranchi grows marigold seedlings in three trays for ten days. Tray 1 stands in the sun and is watered daily. Tray 2 is watered daily but kept under a cardboard box. Tray 3 stands in the sun and is watered only on the first day. The average heights are: tray 1, 18 cm; tray 2, 11 cm; tray 3, 6 cm (and its leaves have turned yellow).
(a) Match each tray to pot A, B or C of Activity 10.1.
(b) How many centimetres taller is tray 1 than tray 2, and than tray 3? Which missing factor lowered the height more in this data?
(c) Does tray 3's yellowing agree with what the book says about pot B?
(d) The school can fix only one problem this week. Using your answers, which should it fix first?
questions.a: (a) Tray 1 is pot A, tray 2 is pot C and tray 3 is pot B. (b) 7 cm taller than tray 2 and 12 cm taller than tray 3; lack of water lowered the height more. (c) Yes. The book says the plant in pot B may die for want of water, so yellow, stunted growth fits. (d) Water first, because the no-water tray did worse (6 cm against 11 cm), but both sunlight and water are needed in the long run.
s: Part (a): trays matched to pots A, C and B
Part (b): correct differences 7 cm and 12 cm and water named
Part (c): links tray 3 to pot B
Part (d): fixes water first using the data and notes both are needed

questions.q: Differentiate between the sapling in pot A and the sapling in pot B of Activity 10.1 in terms of what each was given and what is expected after two weeks.
questions.a: Pot A gets sunlight and water and grows best. Pot B gets sunlight but no water and may die.
s: Pot A: sunlight and water, grows best
Pot B: sunlight but no water, may die

questions.q: Plan a two-pot set-up that tests only the role of sunlight in the growth of a marigold sapling. Say what is kept the same and what is changed.
questions.a: Two pots with same-size saplings and same soil, both watered equally every day. One is kept in direct sunlight and the other in the dark. Observe height and leaves for two weeks.
s: Keeps pots, saplings, soil and water the same
Changes only sunlight: one in sunlight, one in the dark
Says what to observe over two weeks

questions.q: Which statement about plant growth is FALSE?
questions.a: Pot B (sunlight, no water) may die, and pot C (water, no sunlight) grows less, so 'sunlight alone is enough' is false.
o: Sunlight alone is enough for a plant to grow, so watering is optional
A sapling in the dark with water grows less than one in sunlight with water
A sunlit sapling that is never watered may die in a few days
Plants need both sunlight and water for their growth

questions.q: Which set lists changes that the chapter gives as signs of a growing plant?
questions.a: The chapter says that as a plant grows new leaves and branches emerge, its height increases and its stem thickens.
o: New leaves and branches appear, the plant gets taller, the stem thickens
Old leaves are shed, the plant gets taller and its stem gets much thinner
The plant gets taller, but no new leaves or branches ever appear on it
New roots appear underground, while the height and stem stay the same

questions.q: A school gardener has two corners for tomato saplings: a sunny corner far from any tap, where water must be carried in cans, and a shaded corner next to a tap. Using what you know from Activity 10.1, say what each corner offers, what is likely to happen in each if nothing else is done, and recommend a plan.
questions.a: The sunny corner gives sunlight but water must be carried; if not watered the plants are like pot B and may die. The shaded corner has water but no sunlight; plants are like pot C and grow less. Plants need both, so the gardener should use the sunny corner and arrange regular watering with cans, since sunlight cannot be added to the shaded corner by watering.
s: Sunny corner: sunlight but water is a problem, like pot B
Shaded corner: water but no sunlight, like pot C
Likely result in each corner
Recommends the sunny corner with regular watering
Reason: both sunlight and water are needed and water cannot replace sunlight

questions.q: Two chilli saplings are compared for two weeks. One stands on a sunny terrace and is watered daily. The other is in a windowless store room and is watered three times a day. What does the result most likely support?
questions.a: Pot C (water, no sunlight) grows less than pot A. Extra water is not a substitute for sunlight.
o: The store-room plant grows less, so extra water cannot replace sunlight
The store-room plant grows more, because more water gives more growth
Both plants grow equally, because both are watered every day
The terrace plant grows less, because plants should not get sunlight daily

questions.q:
Three similar saplings are kept as follows: X in sunlight with water, Y in sunlight without water, Z in the dark with water.
(a) Which plant is expected to grow the most?
(b) Why can Y and Z not be compared with each other to find the effect of one factor?
questions.a: (a) X. (b) Y and Z differ in both sunlight and water, so any difference could be due to either factor.
s: Part (a): picks X, which gets both sunlight and water
Part (b): explains that Y and Z differ in two conditions at once

questions.q:
Statement 1: As a plant grows, its height increases and its stem thickens.
Statement 2: A sapling kept in the dark with plenty of water grows as well as a sunlit one.
Statement 3: Two pots that differ only in water let us judge the effect of water on growth.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 is false: pot C, in the dark with water, grows less than pot A.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A student sets up only pots A and B of Activity 10.1 and says she can now tell whether sunlight is needed for growth. Show that she cannot.
questions.a: Pots A and B are both in sunlight; they differ only in water. Nothing in the set-up has a plant without sunlight, so the effect of sunlight cannot be judged. A pot in the dark with water (pot C) is needed.
s: Notes that A and B are both in sunlight
States that they differ only in water
Says a pot kept in the dark with water (pot C) is needed

questions.q: The chapter describes the ancient text Vrikshayurveda as a record of
questions.a: It records useful observations about plant growth, soil and agricultural practices, including organic manure preparation.
o: observations on plant growth, soil and farming practices
rules for giving names to plants by the shape of their leaves
dates on which saplings must be planted during festivals
chemical tests for finding starch in the leaves of a plant

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The plant in pot C grows less than the plant in pot A.
Reason (R): Pot C is given water every day.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Pot C gets water just like pot A; it grows less because it gets no sunlight.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: Compare pots A, B and C of Activity 10.1: what each receives and what is expected after two weeks. Then say which pair of pots isolates the effect of water and which pair isolates the effect of sunlight.
questions.a: A: sunlight and water, grows best. B: sunlight, no water, may die. C: water, no sunlight, grows less than A. A and B differ only in water, so that pair isolates water. A and C differ only in sunlight, so that pair isolates sunlight.
s: Pot A: what it gets and grows best
Pot B: what it gets and may die
Pot C: what it gets and grows less
Pair A and B isolates water
Pair A and C isolates sunlight

questions.q:
Match the pot or text with what it stands for in Activity 10.1.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Pot A
2. Pot B
3. Pot C
4. Vrikshayurveda

a. Kept in the dark with water
b. Kept in sunlight with no water
c. Kept in sunlight with water
d. Ancient text with notes on farming
questions.a: Pot A is in sunlight with water, pot B in sunlight without water, pot C in the dark with water, Vrikshayurveda is the ancient text.

questions.q: Meena keeps two similar tomato saplings on a sunny balcony. She waters one every day and never waters the other. After two weeks the unwatered one is drying up. Which idea from Activity 10.1 does this match?
questions.a: The unwatered sunlit sapling matches pot B, which may die.
o: Like pot B: sunlight alone is not enough, and water is also needed
Like pot A, it shows that a sunlit plant grows best even without any water
Like pot C, it shows that a plant kept without sunlight grows less than others
It shows that sunlight is harmful to young saplings in the first two weeks

questions.q:
(a) What does the Vrikshayurveda say about trees and planting, as quoted in the chapter?
(b) Which practice from the text does the chapter name as an example, and what does it mix?
questions.a: (a) Trees do not produce fruits and flowers merely because they are planted. (b) Organic manure preparation, mixing water, barley and seeds such as green, black and horse grams.
s: Part (a): the quoted line
Part (b): organic manure with water, barley and seeds

questions.q: A student wants to test only the effect of water on the growth of chilli saplings. Which of these should be the same in all her pots?
questions.a: A fair test changes one condition (water) and keeps every other condition the same.
o: Sunlight, soil, pot size and size of the sapling
Amount of water given, soil and the pot size
Only the size of the sapling, as light does not matter
Nothing, because the plants adjust to every condition

questions.q:
In Table 10.1 the height of each plant is noted on Day 1 and again after two weeks.
(a) Why is the Day 1 reading needed?
(b) Name two other things, besides height, that are recorded.
questions.a: (a) To see how much the plant has changed by comparing with its starting height. (b) Number of leaves and colour of leaves.
s: Part (a): the starting value shows the change in growth
Part (b): number of leaves and colour of leaves

questions.q: In what form do plants store their food, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Plants store food as starch, which is made in the leaves.
o: Starch, a type of carbohydrate
Chlorophyll, a green pigment
Vitamins, taken up from the soil
Alcohol, a flammable liquid

questions.q: Show that a student who adds iodine to a leaf without decolourising it first cannot read the result reliably.
questions.a: A green leaf's own colour would hide the blue-black colour. The chapter says decolourising enables us to observe the colour change easily. Without it we could not be sure whether starch was present.
s: States the leaf's own colour hides the colour change
Quotes that decolourising makes the change easy to observe
Concludes the presence of starch cannot be judged reliably

questions.q: Justify the statement 'Leaves are the food factories of plants' using the starch test and the test on green and non-green patches.
questions.a: The starch test shows the leaf contains starch, the stored food. In the patch test only the green patches of the sunlit plant's leaf turned blue-black and the dark-kept plant's leaf did not, so starch is made where chlorophyll is present and sunlight is available. Leaves are broad and flat and mostly green, so they capture sunlight efficiently. Hence the food is made in leaves.
s: Starch is found in leaves
Green patches of the sunlit leaf turn blue-black
Dark-kept leaf shows no starch, so sunlight is essential
Chlorophyll is needed, linking to green patches
Broad flat shape and green colour suit capturing sunlight

questions.q:
In a school lab in Kolkata, Ravi decolourises two leaves from a plant that has stood in bright sunlight: a green leaf and a red amaranthus leaf. Both turn blue-black after iodine is added. Ravi writes in his notebook: 'Red leaves have no chlorophyll, and they make starch without it.'
(a) What does the blue-black colour in the red leaf tell you?
(b) Why must the red leaf be decolourised before testing?
(c) Is Ravi's sentence correct? Use what the chapter says about red, violet and brown leaves.
(d) Rewrite his sentence so that it is correct.
questions.a: (a) Starch was made, so photosynthesis took place in the red leaf. (b) Its red pigment would otherwise hide the colour change and make it hard to see. (c) Not correct: red leaves contain other pigments that hide the green, so the leaf may still have chlorophyll, and some of these pigments also help in photosynthesis. (d) Red leaves have other pigments that hide the green colour, and the leaf still makes starch, so photosynthesis takes place in it.
s: Part (a): starch made, photosynthesis took place
Part (b): decolourising makes the colour change easy to see
Part (c): rejects the sentence using the pigment fact
Part (d): writes a corrected sentence

questions.q: Aarav tests the green patches of a leaf taken from a plant that was kept in the dark for 36 hours. What will he see after the iodine test, and why?
questions.a: As in Bhaskar's Activity 10.3, the leaf from the plant in the dark shows no blue-black colour even in its green patches.
o: No blue-black colour, because without sunlight no starch was made
Blue-black colour, because green patches always store starch in them
Blue-black colour, because chlorophyll alone is enough to make starch
The leaf turns colourless, because iodine removes the chlorophyll

questions.q: Which statement about leaves is FALSE?
questions.a: Red, violet or brown leaves have other pigments hiding the green, and some of these pigments also help photosynthesis, so 'can never' is false.
o: A leaf that is not green can never help in making food
Leaves are generally broad and flat in their design
Leaves are mostly green because of the pigment chlorophyll
Leaves are called the food factories of the plants

questions.q: A tulsi plant and a coleus plant with red leaves both stand in sunlight. Plan how you will find out whether each of their leaves has made starch. Write the steps in order, the safety precaution and how you will read the result for each plant.
questions.a: Boil one leaf of each plant in water for five minutes to soften it. Put each in alcohol in a test tube kept in a beaker of boiling water until colourless; never heat alcohol directly. Place each leaf on a plate, add diluted iodine and wait. Blue-black means starch is present, for the tulsi leaf and for the red leaf; the red leaf is tested the same way because other pigments only hide its green.
s: Softening both leaves by boiling in water
Decolourising in alcohol in a beaker of boiling water
Safety: alcohol never heated directly
Adding diluted iodine to each leaf
Reading blue-black as starch for each leaf

questions.q:
A red-leaved plant stands in sunlight. After decolourising, one of its leaves turns blue-black with iodine.
(a) What does this show?
(b) Why does this not contradict the idea that chlorophyll is needed?
questions.a: (a) Starch was made, so photosynthesis took place in that leaf. (b) Red leaves have other pigments that hide the green colour; chlorophyll may still be present, and some of these pigments also help photosynthesis.
s: Part (a): starch made, so photosynthesis took place
Part (b): other pigments hide the green colour

questions.q: Rohan keeps a variegated money-plant leaf, with green and white patches, in a sunny window for a few days. He decolourises it and adds iodine. What is the most likely result?
questions.a: Starch forms where chlorophyll and sunlight are available; non-green patches may not have enough chlorophyll to make detectable starch.
o: The green patches turn blue-black more than the white patches
Only the white patches turn blue-black, as they have no chlorophyll
The whole leaf turns equally blue-black, as sunlight reaches all of it
No patch turns blue-black, as only dark-kept leaves hold starch

questions.q: A leaf turned blue-black with iodine. List three things the plant must have had for it to make the starch found in that leaf.
questions.a: Sunlight, chlorophyll in the leaf, and (as the next activities show) carbon dioxide and water; any three of these.
s: Names sunlight
Names chlorophyll
Names carbon dioxide or water

questions.q:
In the starch test a leaf is first boiled in water and then put in alcohol.
(a) What is the purpose of boiling it in water for five minutes?
(b) How does the purpose of the alcohol step differ?
questions.a: (a) To soften the leaf. (b) The alcohol makes the leaf colourless so that the colour change with iodine is easy to see.
s: Part (a): boiling softens the leaf
Part (b): alcohol decolourises so colour change is easy to see

questions.q: After the iodine test, a part of a decolourised leaf turns blue-black. This tells us that
questions.a: Blue-black with iodine indicates starch.
o: starch is present in that part of the leaf
chlorophyll has been destroyed in that part
alcohol is still left in that part of the leaf
sunlight has been stored in that part

questions.q: Tanya says: 'The green patch of a sunlit leaf turned blue-black because it had chlorophyll and light. The non-green patch did not turn blue-black, so it has no chlorophyll at all.' Agree or disagree with each part.
questions.a: She is right in the first part: starch is made where chlorophyll captures sunlight. The second part goes too far: the non-green patch may not have sufficient chlorophyll to prepare starch that can be detected, which is not the same as having none.
s: First part: agrees, chlorophyll and sunlight make starch
Second part: disagrees, it may only lack sufficient chlorophyll
Reason: test detects only enough starch

questions.q:
Leaves are broad and flat 'by design'.
(a) State how this shape suits the main job of a leaf.
(b) What would be the effect on food-making of a leaf that has little chlorophyll?
questions.a: (a) A broad flat surface can capture more sunlight for making food. (b) Less sunlight would be captured, so less starch would be made.
s: Part (a): broad flat shape captures sunlight for making food
Part (b): little chlorophyll means less capture of sunlight and less starch

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Only the green patches of the leaf from the sunlit plant turned blue-black with iodine.
Reason (R): Chlorophyll helps in capturing sunlight efficiently.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: starch is made where chlorophyll captures sunlight.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: Differentiate between the green patch and the non-green patch of a leaf from a sunlit plant in terms of the iodine test result and the reason.
questions.a: Green patch turns blue-black because it has chlorophyll and made starch. Non-green patch does not turn blue-black; it may not have sufficient chlorophyll to prepare enough starch to be detected.
s: Green patch: blue-black, starch made with chlorophyll
Non-green patch: no blue-black, may not have sufficient chlorophyll

questions.q:
Rani keeps a leaf in alcohol in a test tube inside a beaker of boiling water.
(a) What change will she see in the leaf?
(b) Why must she wait for this change before adding iodine?
questions.a: (a) The leaf becomes colourless. (b) Otherwise the leaf's own colour would hide the blue-black colour, so the starch test could not be read easily.
s: Part (a): the leaf turns colourless
Part (b): the colour change is easy to see only on a colourless leaf

questions.q: What is the job of chlorophyll in a leaf?
questions.a: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that helps capture sunlight; starch is the stored food and iodine turns blue-black with starch.
o: It helps in capturing sunlight efficiently
It stores the food of the leaf in the form of starch
It takes up water and minerals from the soil
It turns blue-black when iodine is added to it

questions.q:
Statement 1: Leaves are mostly green because of a pigment called starch.
Statement 2: Alcohol should never be placed near a heat source directly because it is highly flammable.
Statement 3: Starch, a carbohydrate, is produced in the leaves of a plant.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: the pigment is chlorophyll; starch is the stored food.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A science teacher in Guwahati tests three leaves from similar plants. Leaf L1 is from a plant kept in sunlight for two days. Leaf L2 is from a plant kept in the dark for 36 hours. Leaf L3 is from a sunlit plant, but a strip of black paper was clipped over its middle during the day. After decolourising, L1 turns blue-black all over, L2 shows no blue-black, and L3 turns blue-black except under the paper strip.
(a) Which two results together show that sunlight is needed for starch?
(b) Why does one leaf, L3, show starch in one part and not in another although it has chlorophyll throughout?
(c) The teacher can test one more leaf: a variegated leaf (green and white patches) from a sunlit plant, or a red leaf from a sunlit plant. Which one tells you more about the role of chlorophyll?
(d) Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) L2 (no starch in the dark) and L1 (starch in sunlight); L3 also supports it. (b) The covered strip got no sunlight, so no starch was made there, while the rest of the leaf got sunlight. (c) The variegated leaf. (d) On the variegated leaf green and non-green patches share the same sunlight, so the comparison shows the effect of chlorophyll alone; the red leaf has other pigments and does not isolate chlorophyll.
s: Part (a): L1 and L2, with L3 as support
Part (b): the covered strip received no sunlight
Part (c): picks the variegated leaf
Part (d): justifies with the same-sunlight comparison of patches

questions.q:
Match each item with its role in the starch test.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Chlorophyll
2. Alcohol in a test tube in boiling water
3. Diluted iodine
4. Blue-black colour

a. Colour that shows starch is present
b. Removes the colour of the leaf
c. Green pigment that captures sunlight
d. Dropped on the decolourised leaf
questions.a: Chlorophyll captures sunlight; alcohol removes colour; iodine is dropped on the leaf; blue-black shows starch.

questions.q: Compare Activity 10.4 and Activity 10.5: what each tests, what is observed, and what each shows about photosynthesis.
questions.a: Activity 10.4 tests whether carbon dioxide is needed: the part of the leaf without carbon dioxide does not form starch, so carbon dioxide is essential. Activity 10.5 tests whether a gas is released: the sunlit water plant gives bubbles in which a matchstick burns intensely, so oxygen is released. Both need sunlight. Together: photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.
s: Aim of 10.4: role of carbon dioxide
Result of 10.4: no starch where it was absorbed
Aim and result of 10.5: bubbles and matchstick test
Both are done in sunlight
Joint conclusion: carbon dioxide used, oxygen released

questions.q: Plan an experiment with the water plant, funnel and inverted test tube to find out whether more light gives more oxygen bubbles. State what you change, what you keep the same, what you observe and how you decide.
questions.a: Make identical set-ups with the same kind and size of water plant. Keep one in bright sunlight and another in a shaded place, changing only the amount of light. Keep water and time the same. Count the bubbles that collect in the same time. If the brighter set-up collects more bubbles, more light gives more oxygen.
s: Identical set-ups of the water plant
Changes only the amount of light
Keeps water and time the same
Counts bubbles collected
States how the comparison gives the decision

questions.q: Rahul puts the water plant, funnel and inverted test tube set-up in a dark cupboard instead of sunlight. What does he most likely observe?
questions.a: The set-up in the dark does not give bubbles; photosynthesis occurs in the presence of sunlight.
o: No bubbles collect, because photosynthesis needs sunlight
More bubbles collect, because the plant needs darkness to release oxygen
The same bubbles collect, because oxygen comes from water alone
Bubbles of carbon dioxide collect, because the plant now respires

questions.q:
Match each item with its use in the experiments on carbon dioxide and oxygen.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Caustic soda
2. Lit matchstick
3. Keeping the plant in the dark for 2-3 days
4. Inverted test tube over a funnel

a. Burns intensely in oxygen-rich gas
b. Absorbs carbon dioxide
c. Destarches the plant
d. Collects the gas released
questions.a: Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide; the matchstick shows oxygen; darkness destarches; the test tube collects the gas.

questions.q:
A school in Chennai sets up two identical tomato plants in two transparent plastic tents, both in bright sunlight. Inside tent 1 a small dish of caustic soda is kept. Inside tent 2 a dish of plain water is kept. After a day, a leaf from each plant is decolourised and tested with iodine. The nursery owner asks whether caustic soda could be used in tents to help plants grow bigger.
(a) Predict the iodine result for the leaf from each tent.
(b) Why was a dish of plain water kept in tent 2?
(c) What does the result show about carbon dioxide?
(d) Decide whether the owner should use caustic soda in his tents, with two reasons.
questions.a: (a) Tent 1: no blue-black. Tent 2: blue-black. (b) To keep all conditions the same except the caustic soda, so the difference can be blamed on it. (c) Carbon dioxide from the air is essential for making starch. (d) No. Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide, so the plants would make less food; it is also a strong chemical that can burn skin.
s: Part (a): tent 1 no blue-black, tent 2 blue-black
Part (b): a comparison with only one difference
Part (c): carbon dioxide is essential
Part (d): rejects, with the carbon dioxide and safety reasons

questions.q: Which part of a plant is the primary site of photosynthesis?
questions.a: A leaf is the primary site; other parts with chlorophyll also perform photosynthesis.
o: The leaf, though other green parts also do it
The root, because it takes up the water
The flower, because it is brightly coloured
The seed, because it stores starch for later

questions.q:
(a) Name the four things the chapter lists as essential for the synthesis of food in plants.
(b) Which of the four was tested by using caustic soda?
questions.a: (a) Sunlight, water, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide. (b) Carbon dioxide.
s: Part (a): sunlight, water, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide
Part (b): carbon dioxide

questions.q:
In Activity 10.4 the plant is first kept in the dark for two to three days.
(a) What is the purpose of this step?
(b) What difficulty would arise in reading the result if it were skipped?
questions.a: (a) To destarch the plant so it loses any stored starch. (b) The part inside the bottle might already contain starch and turn blue-black, so we could not tell whether starch was made during the experiment.
s: Part (a): destarching, losing stored starch
Part (b): old starch would confuse the result

questions.q: A report says: 'Bubbles collected in the inverted test tube in the sunlit set-up; a lit matchstick burnt intensely in the gas; the dark set-up gave no bubbles.' Write the aim and the conclusion of the activity.
questions.a: Aim: to find out whether a gas is released during photosynthesis and whether sunlight is needed. Conclusion: oxygen is released during photosynthesis, and photosynthesis occurs in the presence of sunlight.
s: States a suitable aim
Concludes oxygen is released
Concludes sunlight is needed

questions.q:
(a) Apart from the leaf, name one other part of a plant that can photosynthesise.
(b) What must this part contain for it to do so?
questions.a: (a) Any other green part, such as a green stem. (b) Chlorophyll.
s: Part (a): another green part
Part (b): chlorophyll

questions.q:
Statement 1: Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide from the air.
Statement 2: Only the leaf can ever carry out photosynthesis; other green parts cannot.
Statement 3: A lit matchstick burns with an intense flame in the gas collected from a sunlit water plant.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 is false: other parts of the plant that have chlorophyll also perform photosynthesis.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Which of these is NOT needed for photosynthesis?
questions.a: Sunlight, water, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll are essential. Oxygen is released.
o: Oxygen from the surroundings
Sunlight falling on the plant
Water taken up by the plant
Chlorophyll present in the plant

questions.q:
(a) Why should only teachers handle caustic soda?
(b) Name the gas it absorbs and say what the leaf part inside the bottle fails to make because of this.
questions.a: (a) It is a strong chemical that can cause skin burns. (b) Carbon dioxide; the part inside fails to make starch.
s: Part (a): can cause skin burns
Part (b): carbon dioxide absorbed, so no starch inside

questions.q: A leaf with water and chlorophyll is kept in bright sunlight, but completely inside an airtight bottle that also holds caustic soda. Show that it cannot make starch.
questions.a: Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide from the air in the bottle. Carbon dioxide is essential for making starch, so even with sunlight, water and chlorophyll no starch can be made.
s: Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide is essential for starch
So no starch despite sunlight, water and chlorophyll

questions.q: Differentiate between the sunlit and the dark set-up of the water plant with funnel and inverted test tube, in terms of what is seen and what it shows.
questions.a: Sunlit set-up: bubbles collect, the gas is rich in oxygen, so photosynthesis releases oxygen. Dark set-up: no bubbles, showing photosynthesis needs sunlight.
s: Sunlit set-up: bubbles of oxygen
Dark set-up: no bubbles, sunlight is needed

questions.q: A lit matchstick burns with an intense flame in the gas collected from a sunlit water plant. What does this show about the gas?
questions.a: An intense flame shows the gas is rich in oxygen, which is released during photosynthesis.
o: The gas collected is rich in oxygen
The gas collected is rich in carbon dioxide
The gas collected is mostly water vapour from the plant
The gas collected is a mixture with no oxygen in it

questions.q:
Anjali puts two identical sprigs of a water plant under funnels, each with an inverted test tube full of water, in two tumblers. Tumbler S stands on a sunny veranda and tumbler T is covered with a thick black cloth. After one hour, tube S has collected gas that made 28 bubbles pass up while tube T has none. She assumes tube S keeps collecting gas at the same rate.
(a) Name the gas in tube S and say how she can check it.
(b) Why does tube T give none?
(c) How many bubbles does she expect in tube S after 3 hours at the same rate?
(d) For the school science fair, the stage in the sun or the hall in shade is available. Which should Anjali choose for her demonstration, and why?
questions.a: (a) Oxygen; a lit matchstick burns intensely in it. (b) Photosynthesis needs sunlight, and the covered plant gets none. (c) 84 bubbles (28 x 3). (d) The sunny stage, since only a sunlit plant photosynthesises and releases visible oxygen bubbles; the shaded hall would give few or none.
s: Part (a): oxygen, checked with a lit matchstick
Part (b): no sunlight, so no photosynthesis
Part (c): 84 bubbles
Part (d): chooses the sunny stage with a photosynthesis reason

questions.q: In Activity 10.4 the part of the leaf outside the bottle turns blue-black but the part inside does not. What explains this?
questions.a: Both halves had sunlight, water and chlorophyll. Only carbon dioxide was missing inside.
o: Caustic soda absorbed the carbon dioxide inside, so no starch was made there
Water could not reach the part of the leaf inside the bottle at all
Caustic soda removed the chlorophyll from the part inside the bottle
The part inside released oxygen, which stopped the starch from forming

questions.q: Which chemical is placed in the bottle in Activity 10.4 to absorb carbon dioxide from the air?
questions.a: Caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide. Lime water is used in Activity 10.8 to show carbon dioxide; iodine shows starch; alcohol decolourises.
o: Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide)
Lime water, the test for a gas
Diluted iodine, the test for starch
Alcohol, used to remove colour

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A water plant in a dark cupboard gives no bubbles, but one in sunlight does.
Reason (R): Oxygen supports burning, so a lit matchstick flares in oxygen-rich gas.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the reason about burning does not explain why bubbles depend on sunlight; the cause is that photosynthesis needs sunlight.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: Dev says: 'In Activity 10.4 only the half of the leaf inside the bottle teaches us anything, so the half outside the bottle is not needed.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The half outside the bottle has sunlight, water, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide and turns blue-black, so it shows that starch is made when carbon dioxide is available. The inside half, where caustic soda absorbs carbon dioxide, stays unchanged. Only by comparing both halves can we conclude that carbon dioxide is essential.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Outside half turns blue-black, so starch is made when carbon dioxide is present
Comparison with the inside half shows carbon dioxide is essential

questions.q: At noon, a leaf on a sunlit hibiscus plant is making food. Which gases mainly cross its stomata for photosynthesis?
questions.a: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and releases oxygen. Oxygen in and carbon dioxide out is the reverse, typical of respiration.
o: Carbon dioxide goes in and oxygen goes out
Oxygen goes in and carbon dioxide goes out
Water goes in and glucose goes out
Carbon dioxide goes in and starch comes out

questions.q: What is the food actually produced in photosynthesis, and what happens to it later?
questions.a: Glucose is an instant source of energy and is later converted into starch for storage.
o: Glucose, which later gets converted into starch for storage
Starch, which later gets converted into glucose for storage
Chlorophyll, which later gets converted into starch for storage
Glucose, which is always used up at once and is never stored in the plant

questions.q: Explain photosynthesis in a nutshell: what is needed, what is produced, what happens to the product, and which structures help the leaf to exchange gases.
questions.a: Water (taken in by roots), sunlight, carbon dioxide from the air and chlorophyll are needed. Glucose, a simple carbohydrate, and oxygen are produced. Glucose gives instant energy and later gets converted into starch for storage. Stomata on the leaf surface help the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
s: Names the four requirements
Names glucose and oxygen as products
Glucose as instant energy source
Starch storage
Stomata and gas exchange

questions.q:
(a) What is glucose?
(b) Why does the plant convert the glucose it does not use at once into starch?
questions.a: (a) A simple carbohydrate and an instant source of energy. (b) Starch is the form in which food is stored for later use.
s: Part (a): simple carbohydrate, instant energy
Part (b): starch is for storage

questions.q: A plant leaf has produced glucose and oxygen. Write a short note naming two raw materials it must have used and two other things that were needed.
questions.a: Raw materials: carbon dioxide from air and water taken by roots. Also needed: sunlight and chlorophyll.
s: Names carbon dioxide and water
Names sunlight and chlorophyll
Says where carbon dioxide and water come from

questions.q: Sana says: 'Stomata help the plant only in photosynthesis. In respiration no gases need to be exchanged, so stomata play no part.' Do you agree?
questions.a: No. The book says stomata help in the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide during both photosynthesis and respiration. Respiration takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, so gases are exchanged and the same pores serve both.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Stomata help gas exchange in both photosynthesis and respiration
Respiration takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide

questions.q: Following R. H. Dastur's interest in water, temperature and colour of light, plan an investigation of the effect of temperature on photosynthesis in a water plant using a funnel and inverted test tube. State what you change, what you keep the same, what you observe and how you would conclude.
questions.a: Use identical water plants in funnels and inverted test tubes. Change only the temperature of the water in each set-up, keeping sunlight, amount of water and plant size the same. Observe the bubbles of oxygen collecting in the test tubes in the same time. A set-up with more bubbles shows more photosynthesis, so the temperature that gives most bubbles suits it best.
s: Uses identical plants in the funnel set-up
Changes only temperature
Keeps light, water and plants same
Observes oxygen bubbles in the same time
Draws a conclusion from the comparison

questions.q: Which statement about stomata is FALSE?
questions.a: Stomata help in the exchange of both gases, so 'only' and 'never' make the statement false.
o: They allow only carbon dioxide to enter and never allow oxygen to leave
They help in the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in photosynthesis
They also help in gas exchange during respiration of the plant
They can be seen on a peel of the lower leaf surface under a microscope

questions.q: What are stomata?
questions.a: Stomata are pores on leaves. Xylem and phloem are the tube systems; chlorophyll is the pigment.
o: Tiny pores on the leaf surface that help in the exchange of gases
Thin tube-like structures that carry water and minerals upward
Thin tube-like structures that carry food from leaves to roots
A green pigment in leaves that captures the sunlight for food

questions.q:
A nursery owner near Nashik plans to cover the roof of his tomato polyhouse with a coloured sheet to cut the heat. A botanist tells him about the work of Rustom Hormusji Dastur, a plant scientist at the Royal Institute of Science, Bombay, on photosynthesis.
(a) Which three things did Dastur study in relation to photosynthesis?
(b) Which of these does a coloured sheet change most directly?
(c) Describe a small trial using funnels, water plants and inverted test tubes to compare plants under the sheet and in the open.
(d) Should the owner cover the whole roof now? Use your answers.
questions.a: (a) The amount of water, temperature and the colour of light. (b) The colour of the light reaching the plants (and possibly the temperature). (c) Identical water plants, one set-up under the sheet and one in the open; compare the oxygen bubbles collected in the same time. (d) Not yet. Since colour of light and temperature affect photosynthesis, he should run the small trial first and cover the roof only if the plants under the sheet make as much oxygen.
s: Part (a): water, temperature, colour of light
Part (b): colour of light
Part (c): identical set-ups compared by bubbles
Part (d): decides to run the trial before covering, using (b) and (c)

questions.q:
(a) Write the word equation of photosynthesis.
(b) For each substance on the left side, say whether it comes from the soil or the air and through which part of the plant it enters.
questions.a: (a) Carbon dioxide + Water gives Glucose + Oxygen, in sunlight with chlorophyll. (b) Carbon dioxide comes from the air through stomata; water comes from the soil through the roots.
s: Part (a): correct word equation
Part (b): carbon dioxide from air via stomata, water from soil via roots

questions.q:
For Annual Day, Anita's mother in Hyderabad wants to put a shiny coating on the leaves of a money plant. She can coat only the upper surface of each leaf, or both surfaces. In the school lab Anita saw a peel from the lower surface of a leaf under the microscope, stained with a drop of ink.
(a) On which surface of the leaf did the lab activity show the stomata, and what are stomata?
(b) Which two gases pass through stomata in photosynthesis?
(c) Which plan blocks less of what the lab showed, and what does the book not tell us about the upper surface?
(d) Advise Anita: coat the upper surface only for the event, coat both, or coat neither? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The lower surface; stomata are tiny pores that help in the exchange of gases. (b) Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves. (c) Coating only the upper surface, since the stomata were shown on the lower surface; but the book does not say the upper surface has none. (d) Coat only the upper surface, and only for the event, then wash it off; coating both surfaces would block the pores seen in the lab that exchange gases for photosynthesis and respiration.
s: Part (a): lower surface, stomata as pores for gas exchange
Part (b): carbon dioxide in, oxygen out
Part (c): upper-surface-only blocks less and the caution about the upper surface
Part (d): reasoned advice, upper surface only or none

questions.q:
Match each term with its description.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Stomata
2. Glucose
3. R. H. Dastur
4. Starch

a. Plant scientist who studied effects of water, temperature and colour of light
b. Pores for the exchange of gases
c. Simple carbohydrate and instant source of energy
d. Form in which food is stored
questions.a: Stomata are pores; glucose is the simple carbohydrate; Dastur studied photosynthesis; starch is stored food.

questions.q: A researcher wants to find out, as R. H. Dastur did, how temperature affects photosynthesis. Which plan is the best?
questions.a: Only one factor is changed at a time so its effect can be judged.
o: Use the same plants, light and water, and change only the temperature
Change the temperature and the amount of water together in each set-up
Use different kinds of plants at different temperatures and compare them
Change the colour of light at each temperature and ignore the water supply

questions.q:
(a) How are stomata made visible in Activity 10.6?
(b) What job do the pores seen there do for the leaf?
questions.a: (a) A thin peel from the lower surface of a leaf is stained with a drop of ink on a slide and viewed under a microscope. (b) They help in the exchange of gases.
s: Part (a): peel, ink, microscope
Part (b): exchange of gases

questions.q: Which is the correct word equation of photosynthesis?
questions.a: The first wrong option is the equation of respiration; the others mix up the raw materials and products.
o: Carbon dioxide + Water gives Glucose + Oxygen, in sunlight with chlorophyll
Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy, in all living parts
Carbon dioxide + Oxygen gives Glucose + Water + Energy, in sunlight
Water + Glucose gives Carbon dioxide + Oxygen, in the dark with chlorophyll present

questions.q:
(a) Which gas enters a leaf through the stomata for photosynthesis?
(b) Which gas would instead be taken in through the stomata for respiration, and why is it needed?
questions.a: (a) Carbon dioxide. (b) Oxygen, needed to break down glucose to release energy.
s: Part (a): carbon dioxide
Part (b): oxygen, used to break down glucose

questions.q: Show that 'Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water' cannot be the equation of photosynthesis.
questions.a: In photosynthesis carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials and glucose and oxygen are the products, with sunlight and chlorophyll. The given equation has them reversed; it is the respiration equation, which also releases energy.
s: States the raw materials of photosynthesis
States the products and conditions, reversed in the given equation
Identifies the given equation as respiration

questions.q: Differentiate between glucose and starch in a plant in terms of what each is used for.
questions.a: Glucose is the food produced in photosynthesis and an instant source of energy. Starch is the form in which extra glucose is stored.
s: Glucose: instant energy source made in photosynthesis
Starch: storage form made from glucose

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The oxygen released during photosynthesis leaves the leaf into the air.
Reason (R): Stomata are tiny pores on the surface of leaves that help in the exchange of gases.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true; stomata are the pores through which the gases are exchanged, so the reason explains the assertion.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Statement 1: Glucose is a simple carbohydrate that can act as an instant source of energy.
Statement 2: Water and minerals are taken up by the roots of a plant.
Statement 3: Stomata help in gas exchange in photosynthesis but not in respiration.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 is false: stomata help in the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and respiration.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: The food made in the leaves reaches the seeds and roots through
questions.a: The food prepared in the leaves is carried through the phloem and may be stored in seeds and roots.
o: the phloem, a set of thin tube-like structures
the xylem, another set of thin tube-like structures
the stomata, which are tiny pores on the leaf surface
the root hairs, which take up water from the soil

questions.q: Hardeep says: 'The food a plant needs reaches its leaves from the roots through the xylem.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. Roots send water and minerals through the xylem to the leaves. The food is made in the leaves and the phloem carries it from the leaves to all parts.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Xylem carries water and minerals
Food is made in leaves and moved by phloem

questions.q:
Statement 1: The phloem carries water and minerals up from the roots.
Statement 2: Food may be stored in parts of a plant such as seeds and roots.
Statement 3: Minerals dissolved in water also move up through the xylem.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: water and minerals move up through the xylem; the phloem carries food.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: In Activity 10.7, red ink is added to the water in one tumbler so that
questions.a: The red colour travels with the water and shows where the water goes, in the xylem.
o: the path of the water in the stem and flowers can be seen
the plant receives red food to store in its flowers and leaves
the xylem is changed into phloem for the whole day
the roots take up more minerals from the tumbler of water

questions.q: Which statement about transport in plants is FALSE?
questions.a: Water and minerals move up through the xylem, so 'only through the phloem' is false.
o: Water and minerals move upward in a plant only in the phloem
Xylem is present in the stem, branches and the leaves of plants
Food may be stored in parts of a plant such as seeds and roots
Phloem carries the food made in leaves to all parts of the plant

questions.q: Differentiate between xylem and phloem in terms of what each carries and where it comes from.
questions.a: Xylem carries water and minerals taken up by the roots. Phloem carries food made in the leaves.
s: Xylem: water and minerals from the roots
Phloem: food from the leaves

questions.q:
(a) Where is food made in a plant?
(b) If all the leaves of a bean plant are removed early, what happens to the food that could have been stored in its seeds, and why?
questions.a: (a) In the leaves. (b) Less food would be available to store in the seeds, because the food is made in the leaves and carried to the seeds by the phloem.
s: Part (a): leaves
Part (b): less food reaches the seeds as leaves make the food

questions.q: Which tubes carry water and minerals from the roots to other parts of a plant?
questions.a: Xylem transports water and minerals; phloem carries food.
o: Xylem
Phloem
Stomata
Chlorophyll

questions.q: Compare the transport of water and minerals with the transport of food in a plant. Write what carries each, where it starts and where it goes, and where food may be stored.
questions.a: Water and minerals: taken up from the soil by roots, carried through the xylem in the stem, branches and leaves to other parts. Food: made in the leaves by photosynthesis, carried through the phloem to all parts of the plant, and may be stored in parts such as seeds and roots.
s: Tube for water and minerals: xylem
Starts at the roots, goes up to other parts
Tube for food: phloem
Starts at the leaves, goes to all parts
Storage in seeds and roots

questions.q:
(a) Which tubes in the stem carried the red ink in Activity 10.7?
(b) Why would minerals from the soil travel through the same tubes?
questions.a: (a) The xylem. (b) Minerals dissolve in water, and water together with the minerals moves up through the xylem.
s: Part (a): xylem
Part (b): minerals travel dissolved in water through xylem

questions.q:
Ravi cuts a stem of a white balsam twig that stood overnight in red ink water. He cuts thin slices near the base, near the middle and near the top of the stem. Each slice shows red dots when seen with a magnifying glass, and the veins of the leaves are red too. His friend says, 'These red dots are the tubes that carry food.'
(a) What do red dots at all three heights tell you about the route of the ink?
(b) Name the tubes that hold the red dots.
(c) Evaluate the friend's statement.
(d) Ravi also wants to show where food is stored. Which kind of plant parts could he test, and with which test from the book's earlier activity?
questions.a: (a) The ink moved up the whole length of the stem, along thin tubes. (b) The xylem. (c) Wrong: the ink moves with water upward in the xylem, whereas food is carried by the phloem. (d) Seeds or roots, which can store food, tested for starch with iodine.
s: Part (a): ink travelled up through the whole stem
Part (b): xylem
Part (c): the friend is wrong, xylem carries water, phloem carries food
Part (d): seeds or roots tested with iodine for starch

questions.q:
A farmer in Odisha grows radish, a root vegetable, and also sells the leaves as greens. A trader offers to buy half the leaves of every plant at a good price this week. The farmer worries about the size of the radish roots and also about the dry soil.
(a) Where is the food of the radish plant made?
(b) By which tubes does that food reach the root?
(c) By which tubes does water from the soil reach the leaves?
(d) Should he sell half the leaves now? Weigh the trade-off using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) In the leaves. (b) The phloem. (c) The xylem. (d) Selling half the leaves brings money now but leaves fewer food factories to send food through the phloem to the root, so the roots may grow smaller; he should sell only a few leaves, or only if he can accept smaller radishes, and water the soil so the xylem can keep supplying the remaining leaves.
s: Part (a): leaves
Part (b): phloem
Part (c): xylem
Part (d): weighs money against smaller roots using leaves, phloem and xylem

questions.q: Why do plants need the minerals that their roots take in, and how do the minerals reach the leaves?
questions.a: Minerals are important nutrients for the growth of plants. Dissolved in water they move up through the xylem.
s: Minerals are important nutrients for growth
They move up dissolved in water through the xylem

questions.q:
(a) In which direction does water move in the xylem?
(b) From where does the food in the phloem start, and where does it go?
questions.a: (a) Upward from the roots to other parts. (b) From the leaves to all parts of the plant.
s: Part (a): from roots upward to other parts
Part (b): from leaves to all parts

questions.q: Design an experiment with white-flowered twigs and red ink to find out whether water moves up a stem faster in warm or in cold conditions. State what you change, what you keep the same, what you observe and how you decide.
questions.a: Take two twigs of the same plant, cut obliquely under water, and place each in a tumbler with the same amount of red ink water. Keep one tumbler in a warm place and the other in a cold place, changing only the temperature. Keep the plant, ink, amount of water and time the same. After a fixed time, compare how far the red colour has risen in the stem, leaves and flowers. The twig where the red colour has risen higher shows faster water movement.
s: Same plant twigs in tumblers of red ink water
Changes only temperature, warm against cold
Keeps ink, amount of water and time the same
Observes how far the red colour has risen
Decides: higher red colour means faster transport

questions.q: Pooja finds that a carrot, which is a root, is full of stored food. Which explanation matches the chapter?
questions.a: Food made in leaves is transported by the phloem and may be stored in parts such as roots and seeds.
o: The food was made in the leaves and carried to the root by the phloem
The root made the food from the soil by itself and then stored it
The food was carried up from the soil to the root through the xylem
The food came into the root directly from the air around it

questions.q: All the leaves of a young bean plant are below a point on its stem, and its pods are above that point. A gardener cuts through the phloem at that point, leaving the xylem. Show that the pods cannot receive food from those leaves through the stem.
questions.a: Food is made in the leaves and travels to other parts through the phloem. With the phloem cut between the leaves and pods, the food cannot pass the cut, so the pods cannot get food from those leaves by that route.
s: Food is made in the leaves
Phloem is the route for food to other parts
The cut blocks the route to the pods

questions.q: After a day, a student sees red colour in the stem, leaves and flowers of a white-flowered twig and red dots in the cut stem. Describe the experiment she did.
questions.a: She took two tumblers one-third full of water and put red ink in one. She cut the stems of two similar twigs with white flowers obliquely under water and put one in each tumbler, then observed them the next day. A cut upper stem showed red in the xylem.
s: Tumblers with plain water and with red ink
Cut twigs with white flowers placed in each
Observation next day and cut stem showing xylem

questions.q: Seema places a white balsam twig in red ink water overnight. Next day she cuts a thin slice from the upper part of the stem, far above the water, and looks at it with a magnifying glass. What does she see?
questions.a: The ink travels in the xylem, the thin tubes that carry water and minerals.
o: Red colour in the thin tube-like structures called xylem
Red colour spread evenly over the whole slice of stem
Red colour only in the outer skin of the stem
Red colour in the phloem, since the ink is a kind of food

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The flowers of a white-flowered twig kept in red ink water turn red.
Reason (R): The roots of a plant take up water and minerals from the soil.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion: the twig has no roots in the tumbler; the ink rises because the cut stem has xylem that carries water upward.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Match each part with its job in the transport of materials in a plant.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Xylem
2. Phloem
3. White flower in red ink
4. Roots

a. Carries food made in the leaves
b. Carries water and minerals upward
c. Take up water and minerals from the soil
d. Turns red after one day
questions.a: Xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries food; the flower turns red; roots take up water and minerals.

questions.q: Gaurav says: 'The red colour reached the flower through thin tubes in the stem.' Is he right? Explain using Activity 10.7.
questions.a: Yes. A cut stem showed red colour in thin tube-like structures called xylem, which carry water and minerals from the root-end to the stem, branches, leaves and flowers. The ink moved with the water in them.
s: Verdict: agrees
Red seen in thin tubes of the cut stem
Names xylem as carrying water, so the ink travels with it

questions.q: Which gas turns lime water milky?
questions.a: In Activity 10.8, lime water turns milky due to more carbon dioxide.
o: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen gas
Water vapour
Glucose sugar

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The lime water connected to the flask of germinating seeds turned milky.
Reason (R): The germinating seeds took in carbon dioxide from the air in the flask.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The assertion is true, but the reason is false: seeds release carbon dioxide through respiration.
o: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: Which equation shows respiration in plants?
questions.a: The first wrong option is photosynthesis; the second reverses the roles of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
o: Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy
Carbon dioxide + Water gives Glucose + Oxygen + Energy
Glucose + Carbon dioxide gives Oxygen + Water + Energy
Oxygen + Water + Energy gives Glucose + Carbon dioxide

questions.q: Which statement about respiration in plants is FALSE?
questions.a: All parts of a plant respire, so 'only the green parts' is false.
o: Only green parts respire; roots and other non-green parts do not
Glucose is broken down using oxygen to release energy for the plant
Carbon dioxide and water are released along with the energy
All parts of a plant, green or non-green, carry out respiration

questions.q: The energy released in a plant's respiration is used for
questions.a: The energy produced during respiration is used by plants for growth and development.
o: its growth and development
making chlorophyll from sunlight
producing oxygen for the air
absorbing carbon dioxide through stomata

questions.q: Neha says: 'Photosynthesis and respiration are the reverse of each other, so a plant needs only one of them.' Evaluate her claim by comparing the two processes.
questions.a: The equations look reversed: photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and gives glucose and oxygen; respiration uses glucose and oxygen and gives carbon dioxide, water and energy. But they do different jobs and occur in different places. Photosynthesis happens in green parts in sunlight and makes food. Respiration happens in all living parts and releases energy for growth. A plant needs both.
s: Photosynthesis: materials and products
Respiration: materials and products
Where and when each happens
Different jobs: food made versus energy released
Verdict: needs both

questions.q:
In Activity 10.8 one test tube of lime water is joined to the flask with germinating seeds and a second test tube is left unconnected.
(a) Which one turns milky?
(b) What does the clear second tube tell us about the source of the carbon dioxide?
questions.a: (a) The one joined to the flask. (b) The carbon dioxide does not come from the lime water or the air alone; the extra carbon dioxide is produced by the seeds as they respire.
s: Part (a): the connected tube
Part (b): the seeds are the source of extra carbon dioxide

questions.q: A report concludes: 'Soaked moong seeds produce carbon dioxide.' Describe the set-up and the observation that gave this conclusion.
questions.a: Soaked moong seeds on wet cotton in a conical flask, mouth corked and connected by tubes to a test tube of lime water, kept in the dark for 24 hours. The lime water turned milky.
s: Seeds on wet cotton in a flask kept in the dark for 24 hours
Flask connected to lime water
Observation: lime water turns milky

questions.q: Photosynthesis and respiration are essential to maintain balance in nature. Discuss, using the example of a plant sealed in a transparent bottle.
questions.a: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and releases oxygen; respiration uses oxygen and glucose and releases carbon dioxide. In a sealed bottle garden that is growing well, the carbon dioxide produced in respiration is used for photosynthesis, and the oxygen generated in photosynthesis is used in respiration. Each process supplies what the other needs, so gases stay in balance.
s: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and gives oxygen
Respiration uses oxygen and gives carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide from respiration is used in photosynthesis
Oxygen from photosynthesis is used in respiration
Concludes the two keep the exchange of gases in balance

questions.q: A spider plant is grown well in a large transparent bottle and then the mouth of the bottle is sealed. It keeps growing well for weeks in the light. Which idea best explains this?
questions.a: The book says gases are exchanged inside the bottle: carbon dioxide from respiration is used in photosynthesis, and oxygen from photosynthesis is used in respiration.
o: Each process supplies the gas the other needs: carbon dioxide and oxygen
It needs no gases once sealed, since it makes its food only from soil minerals
Photosynthesis and respiration are one process, so no gas in the bottle changes
Oxygen from respiration is used in photosynthesis, which in turn gives carbon dioxide

questions.q:
(a) Where does photosynthesis take place in a plant?
(b) A root is under the soil and non-green. Can it respire? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) In green parts in sunlight. (b) Yes; all parts of a plant, green or non-green, carry out respiration.
s: Part (a): green parts in sunlight
Part (b): yes, all parts respire including non-green ones

questions.q:
(a) Write the word equation of respiration.
(b) Which of the substances on the left comes into the leaf from the air, and through which structures?
questions.a: (a) Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. (b) Oxygen, through the stomata, which help in the exchange of gases in respiration.
s: Part (a): correct word equation
Part (b): oxygen, through stomata

questions.q: A storekeeper in Agra says: 'Potatoes in my dark godown are not green, so they are not respiring.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: The book states that all parts of a plant, green or non-green, carry out respiration.
o: All plant parts respire, green or not, so potatoes do too
Only green plant parts respire in sunlight, so he is right about this
Non-green parts respire only after they turn green once again
Potatoes photosynthesise in the dark and so need no respiration at all

questions.q:
A Class 7 group in Pune sets up two sealed transparent bottles on a sunny window sill. Bottle P holds soil and a healthy spider plant. Bottle Q holds the same soil but no plant. After six weeks the plant in P is still green and growing. A student suggests moving P into a dim cupboard so that it will not get too hot.
(a) Which gas used in photosynthesis is supplied inside bottle P, and by which process of the plant?
(b) Which gas used in respiration is supplied inside bottle P, and by which process?
(c) What would happen to the food-making of the plant in the dim cupboard, and to its respiration?
(d) Should the group move P to the cupboard? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Carbon dioxide, supplied by respiration. (b) Oxygen, supplied by photosynthesis. (c) Photosynthesis would slow down with less sunlight, but respiration in all parts would continue. (d) No. With less sunlight less food is made and less oxygen released while respiration continues to use glucose and oxygen, so the plant would not keep the exchange of gases going.
s: Part (a): carbon dioxide from respiration
Part (b): oxygen from photosynthesis
Part (c): photosynthesis falls, respiration goes on
Part (d): says no, using the gas exchange argument

questions.q: Differentiate between photosynthesis and respiration in terms of what each uses and what each gives.
questions.a: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and gives glucose and oxygen. Respiration uses glucose and oxygen and gives carbon dioxide, water and energy.
s: Photosynthesis: raw materials and products
Respiration: raw materials and products

questions.q: Rakesh says: 'Roots are under the soil and never get sunlight, so respiration cannot occur in roots.' Show that he is wrong.
questions.a: Roots are non-green parts. The chapter says all parts of a plant, green or non-green, carry out respiration. Respiration breaks glucose down with oxygen, so roots can respire.
s: Roots are non-green parts
All parts, green or non-green, respire
So roots respire, using glucose and oxygen

questions.q:
(a) In which area of plant life did Kamala Sohonie do remarkable work?
(b) State what that process releases from glucose.
questions.a: (a) Respiration in plants. (b) It releases energy (with carbon dioxide and water) from glucose.
s: Part (a): respiration in plants
Part (b): releases energy from glucose

questions.q:
Match each item with the correct description.
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Photosynthesis
2. Respiration
3. Lime water
4. Kamala Sohonie

a. Occurs in green parts in sunlight
b. Uses glucose and oxygen
c. Turns milky with carbon dioxide
d. Did remarkable work on respiration in plants
questions.a: Photosynthesis is in green parts in sunlight; respiration uses glucose and oxygen; lime water turns milky; Sohonie worked on respiration.

questions.q:
In a school lab in Coimbatore, two flasks are kept in the dark for 24 hours. Flask 1 holds soaked chana seeds on wet cotton. Flask 2 holds only wet cotton of the same amount. Each is joined by a tube to its own test tube of lime water. Next morning the lime water joined to one flask is milky and the other is clear. A student says, 'The wet cotton must have made the lime water milky.'
(a) Which flask is joined to the milky lime water?
(b) What is the gas, and what produced it?
(c) What is the purpose of flask 2?
(d) Judge the student's statement using the result.
questions.a: (a) Flask 1, with the seeds. (b) Carbon dioxide, produced by the seeds as they respire. (c) Flask 2 shows the effect of the wet cotton alone, to compare with the flask with seeds. (d) The statement is wrong: the flask with cotton alone left its lime water clear, so the cotton did not cause it; the seeds' respiration did.
s: Part (a): flask 1
Part (b): carbon dioxide from respiring seeds
Part (c): flask 2 is the comparison
Part (d): rejects the claim using the clear lime water

questions.q: Tina says: 'Only the green parts of a plant respire, because only they have chlorophyll. The carbon dioxide they release can be used in photosynthesis.' Do you agree?
questions.a: Partly right. The second statement is correct: in the bottle garden, carbon dioxide from respiration is used in photosynthesis. The first is wrong: all parts of a plant, green or non-green, respire, because respiration needs glucose and oxygen, not chlorophyll.
s: Verdict: partly right
Wrong part: all parts, green or non-green, respire
Right part: carbon dioxide from respiration is used in photosynthesis

questions.q:
Statement 1: Respiration in plants occurs only in green parts in sunlight.
Statement 2: Photosynthesis uses glucose and oxygen and gives carbon dioxide and water.
Statement 3: The energy released in respiration is used by plants for growth and development.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: all parts respire. 2 is false: these are the materials and products of respiration.
o: 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
